title: How to Create a Retirement Plan if You’ve Been Self-Employed Your Entire Career
description: Exit strategies for business owners with no pension.
content:
For lifelong entrepreneurs and freelancers, retirement planning is doubly hard. You don't have a pension or employer match, and your net worth is often tied up in the business itself. The common assumption—'I'll sell the business to fund my retirement'—is a high-risk gamble. Most small businesses are hard to sell. The prudent strategy is to skim profits *during* your career to build an independent investment portfolio. This guide explains how to diversify away from your business risk.

Key Takeaways

  • Diversification is Survival: Your business is your income source. If your retirement savings are also reinvested in the business, you have 'Single Point of Failure' risk. You must siphon cash OUT to the stock market.
  • The Solo 401(k): The most powerful tool for self-employed. You can contribute ~$69k/year. Use high-profit years to make massive contributions.
  • Valuation Reality Check: Assume your business is worth $0 at retirement. If you can sell it, that's a bonus. If you can't, your Solo 401(k) must support you.
  • Social Security Audit: If you aggressively wrote off expenses to show low income on tax returns, your Social Security check will be tiny. You need a larger personal portfolio to compensate.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Many business owners suppress their taxable income to save taxes today. The downside is a lower Social Security record. You traded a government annuity for current cash flow. You must invest that cash flow, or you lose on both ends.

The 'Exit' Options

How does a founder actually retire?

Option 1: The Sale (Lump Sum)

Pros: Immediate cash. Clean break.
Cons: Hard to find a buyer. Valuation is often 2-3x EBITDA (low). Taxes on sale are high.
Strategy: Groom a successor or explore an ESOP (Employee Stock Ownership Plan) 5 years in advance.

Option 2: The Passive Owner (Income Stream)

Hire a GM to run it. You take a quarterly profit distribution.
Pros: Continued income. You keep the asset.
Cons: You are never truly 'retired'. You still have liability and oversight duties.

Option 3: The Liquidation (Asset Sale)

Sell the client list, equipment, and real estate. Close the doors.
Pros: Simple.
Cons: Lowest payout. Usually pennies on the dollar.

Building the 'Outside' Pot

  1. Automated Skim: Set up a rule. 10% of Gross Revenue (not profit) goes to a personal wealth account. Treat it like a supplier bill.
  2. Real Estate Diversification: If your business owns its building, put the building in a separate LLC. When you retire, sell the business but keep the building. Charge the new owner rent. This is the safest retirement pension.
  3. Defined Benefit Plan: For high earners ($300k+), you can set up a Defined Benefit plan on top of a Solo 401(k) to shelter $100k+ per year tax-deferred.
  4. Succession Planning: If you want to sell, start documenting processes now. A business that runs without you is valuable. A business that is you is worthless.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I sell to my kids?

Yes, but don't gift it if you need the money. Use an 'Installment Sale'. They pay you monthly from the business profits over 10 years. It acts like a pension.

What if I have no savings?

You must work longer or sell the business aggressively. The 'business is my retirement' plan only works if there is a buyer. Get a valuation today.

Should I buy commercial real estate?

Yes. Owning the building your business occupies is a classic wealth builder. The tenant (your business) pays off the mortgage. You retire with a paid-off income-generating property.
